paper_title: SAE Interprets MoE: Sparse AutoEncoders Reveal That MoE Experts Exhibit Human-Interpretable Fine-Grained Specialization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models route each token to a few of many experts, yet what an individual expert is responsible for remains unsettled. Existing analyses count how often an expert is selected on domain-labeled corpora, an instrument that fixes the taxonomy in advance, stays coarse, and records selection rather than contribution. We instead study specialization in feature space by training a sparse autoencoder (SAE) on the output of an MoE layer. Since this output is a router-weighted sum of expert outputs and the SAE encoder is affine, the pre-activation of every latent decomposes exactly over the experts. Aggregated over a corpus, this gives each expert a dominant set of latents whose activation it principally drives. On layers 4, 30 and 46 of Qwen3-30B-A3B, contribution is far more concentrated than gating, most latents have only one or two dominators, and the overlap between dominant sets concentrates on a few expert pairs. Auto-interpreting these sets reveals a division of labor below coarse domains, with distinct experts for Java and front-end web code, or for geometry and for arithmetic and polynomials, while the coarse domains themselves take very unequal numbers of experts. Our SAEs and code are available at https://github.com/Bytedance-Seed/SAE-Interprets-MoE.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures underlie much of the recent progress in large language models. By routing each token to small subset of experts, an MoE model scales its parameter count, and with it the knowledge and capacity it can store, while keeping per-token inference cost close to that of far smaller dense model. Central to this design is the router, yet the mechanism it implements has received comparatively little scrutiny. How trained model allocates tokens across experts, and hence what any individual expert comes to be responsible for, remains poorly understood. The existing evidence is mixed. Some work reports that experts are domain-specialized, activating preferentially on data drawn from particular domains [11, 14]. Another concludes that routing is unrelated to domains as humans conceive of them, and is instead driven by surface properties such as token identity [10, 18]. What they do share is an instrument, namely counting how often each expert fires on corpora carrying human-assigned 1 Figure 1 An MoE layer outputs router-weighted sum of its active experts (left), and since the SAE encoder is affine, each latents activation decomposes exactly over these experts (middle). Thresholding the contribution fractions averaged over corpus gives the dominance graph (right), and auto-interpreting the latents an expert dominates describes its role (bottom), such as Java expert (E50) and front-end web expert (E57) at layer 30 of Qwen3-30B-A3B. labels, such as GitHub for code or arXiv for academic. This instrument has four limitations: (a) The taxonomy is imposed by the analyst rather than recovered from the model; such study can only ask whether the models division of labor agrees with partition chosen in advance, instead of the organization the model actually learned. (b) The labels available at corpus scale are coarse, typically handful of categories such as code and math. This is far coarser than the division of labor one would expect among the tens to hundreds of experts in single layer. (c) The label attaches to corpus while the routing decision being measured is made per token. For example, math problem statement may contain great deal of story narrative framing, and counting every token of it toward math blurs precisely the distinctions the analysis is meant to detect. (d) Activation frequency records which experts were selected, without regard to the router coefficients that weight them. An expert can be selected on token and still account for little of what the layer computes there. We propose to study expert specialization in the feature space of the model layer. We train Sparse AutoEncoder (SAE; 9) on the output of an MoE layer. SAE latents approximate the features the model itself uses, and are discovered from its activations rather than stipulated in advance. Moreover, they also admit natural decomposition into the contributions of individual experts. The output of an MoE layer is router-weighted sum of the outputs of the active experts; because the SAE encoder is affine in that sum, each latents pre-activation decomposes exactly over the experts that produced it. This yields, for every (expert, latent, token) triple, the share of the latents activation contributed by that expert, which we aggregate over corpus into an expert-level contribution profile. Figure 1 gives an overview, from the decomposition of latents activation over experts to the account of an experts role that it supports. Our approach differs from prior analyses along two axes. In the unit of analysis, we replace analyst-defined domains with latents the SAE learns unsupervised, so the resulting account of specialization is not constrained by taxonomy chosen in advance, and it is finer-grained than any label set that can be assigned at corpus scale. In resolution, we replace corpus-level selection frequency with per-token, per-expert contribution 2 score, which both avoids attributing every token of document to single domain and measures functional contribution rather than mere co-occurrence. We instantiate this analysis on layers 4, 30, and 46 of Qwen3-30B-A3B [19], chosen to cover shallow, mid-late, and deep positions in the network. Our first observation is that contribution is highly concentrated. Most latents receive the bulk of their activation from small number of experts. Building on this, we say that an expert dominates latent when it is principal contributor to that latents activation, and we collect, for each expert, the set of latents it dominates. Interpreting the latents in an experts dominant set therefore describes what that expert does in the models own vocabulary rather than in categories chosen in advance. We obtain such interpretations by auto-interpreting each latent from activating contexts and logit effects (Section J). Most pairs of dominant sets share almost nothing, the overlap that exists concentrates on few pairs of experts, and about half of each experts set is its own. Reading these sets yields two further findings. First, experts specialize at granularity well below that of conventional domain labels; for instance, we identify experts whose dominant set consists primarily of latents on front-end web code rather than on code in general. Second, summarizing the sets into coarse domains shows that the allocation of experts across domains is strongly unequal. Together these show that the experts of this model do divide labor, but along feature-level distinctions rather than the domain-level partitions under which specialization has previously been sought.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Expert specialization in MoE models. Prior analyses report either domain-specialized experts [11, 14] or routing driven by surface properties such as token identity [10, 18], and both rest on selection counts over domain-labeled corpora, whose limitations we discuss in Section 1. recent work leaves the domain level behind. Motivated by k-sparse probing, which finds the neurons inside an expert less polysemantic than those of comparable dense network, it labels hundreds of whole experts automatically and concludes that they are fine-grained task experts rather than domain specialists or token-level processors [8]. Its specialization score is computed against clusters of the models own output embedding, which keeps the categories model-derived, but the number of clusters is hand-set grid of few values, so the score reports which of the chosen resolutions fits an expert best rather than the level at which the model has drawn its division of labor. Our units are learned by the SAE without supervision, so an experts dominant set is read off instead of being matched against partition fixed in advance, and the level at which that set is coherent is itself one of our results. SAEs, interpretability and tracing. Our unit of analysis comes from dictionary learning. Since model holds more features than it has dimensions, placing them in superposition [5], its neurons are polysemantic, and an SAE instead learns an overcomplete sparse dictionary whose directions are considerably more monosemantic [9], construction since scaled to frontier models and to millions of latents [6, 17]. We adopt the top-k variant of Gao et al. [6] in Section 3.2 and read latents by auto-interpretation from activating contexts and logit effects (Section J), following Paulo et al. [16]. Latents also serve to trace computation, in sparse feature circuits [13] and attribution graphs [1], which take latents as nodes and attributions between them as edges. Our attribution runs along different axis, because those works trace computation across layers and components whereas we decompose the activation of one latent within single layer over the experts that produced it. The decomposition of the pre-activation is also exact rather than approximate, since Equation (5) follows algebraically from the linearity of the layer output in the expert outputs.

3.5 Dominance graph
Given a threshold τ , s(j, i) ≥ τ indicates that j generally makes a substantial contribution to i; in this case
we say that j dominates i. We define the dominant set of an expert j to be the set consisting of all latents
dominated by j, denoted S(j) = { i | i is dominated by j }.
sections.content: We construct bipartite graph G(U, V, E), whose left vertex set is the expert set and whose right vertex set is the latent set of the SAE. Its edge set is = { (j, i) U, S(j) }. We call this bipartite graph the dominance graph.

sections.title: 4 Qwen3-30B-A3B has specialized experts
sections.content: We apply Section 3 to layers 4, 30, and 46 of Qwen3-30B-A3B, which we select to represent the models shallow, mid-late, and deep-layer behaviors. The model has 48 layers in total, where each MoE layer of this model contains = 128 experts, with = 8 experts activated per token and no shared experts. We train one individual SAE with latent size of 220 for each of the three layers. Statistics are computed on validation set of 1.5B tokens that shares the same distribution as the SAE training set and has no data overlap with it. Every latent of each SAE activates at least once on this set, so s(j, i) is defined for all latents.

sections.title:
4.1 Contribution is more concentrated than gating
The contribution defined in Equation (6) carries gj(t) as a factor, and the gating weights are themselves
unevenly distributed. The router takes the top-k experts and renormalizes their weights, so higher-ranked
experts naturally receive larger gj(t). Before adopting this statistic we therefore have to rule out a trivial
explanation, namely that the unevenness of the contribution across the activated experts is merely a direct
projection of the unevenness of the gating, and has nothing to do with whether an expert has any preference
over latents.
sections.content: We compare the profiles that the two quantities form once aggregated by rank. For each prefix x1:t we sort the gating weights of the 8 activated experts in descending order, take the value in position (r = 0, . . . , 7), and average it over the entire validation set; we denote the result by gr. Analogously, for each (prefix, activated latent) pair (x1:t, i) with F(t), we sort the 8 values C(j, i, x1:t) in descending order, take the value in position r, and average it over all such pairs; we denote the result by Cr. Note that position need not correspond to the same expert from one case to the next, because what we aggregate is the rank. The two profiles are directly comparable, because the renormalization performed by the router together with the definition in Equation (7) gives (cid:80)k1 Cr = 1. The two profiles thus distribute one and the same total. r=0 gr = (cid:80)k1 r=0 Figure 2 reports the results for the three layers, and in all three Cr is markedly steeper than gr. Taking layer 30 as an example, the first three gating values are 0.231, 0.169 and 0.137, decaying gently, whereas the first three contribution values are 0.512, 0.185 and 0.115, the first of them alone accounting for more than half of the total. The two curves cross between = 1 and = 2, beyond which the contribution stays below the gating throughout; by = 7 we have C7 = 0.005 while g7 = 0.074. Layers 4 and 46 exhibit the same shape. The ReLU in Equation (6) could also steepen Cr, since truncated expert receives = 0 and the remaining experts share the whole unit among themselves. The truncation is mild, however. Of the 8 activated experts of (prefix, activated latent) pair, on average only 2.09, 1.29 and 1.64 are truncated at layers 4, 30 and 46, so most activated experts keep positive contribution and the truncation is not the main source of the steepness. The concentration of the contribution is therefore not an artifact of the top-k routing structure. While the gating profile decays gently, the contribution is highly concentrated on small number of experts.

sections.title: 5 Label experts with latent explanations
sections.content: Section 4 establishes that every expert holds dominant set of latents, that about half of this set is dominated by that expert alone, and that substantial overlap occurs only between few pairs of experts. The set attached to an expert is therefore description of that expert, so interpreting the latents it contains tells us which features the expert is chiefly responsible for. Section 4.2 and Section 4.3 further show that the structure of dominance and its trends are the same at layers 4, 30 and 46, and we therefore report only layer 30 in the rest of this section.

sections.title: 5.1 Dominant-set explanations carry more information than tokens
sections.content: For every expert we sample 2000 latents uniformly from its dominant set, taking the whole set when it holds fewer than 2000 latents. Each sampled latent is interpreted by GPT-5.5 from activating contexts and logit effects, following the pipeline described in Section J. Reading the resulting explanations expert by expert, we find that for most experts they concentrate on few themes. To make this concentration visible at glance, we render the explanations of each expert as word cloud, in which the size of word is its frequency among the explanations of that experts dominant set. Figure 3 shows the explanation word clouds of experts 50, 57 and 93 of layer 30 (a Java expert, front-end web expert and an expert on natural geography and weather), and the word clouds of the remaining experts are collected in Section K. We compare this construction with word cloud drawn directly from the tokens routed to an expert. Ours differs in two respects. The dominant set keeps only the latents the expert principally drives, which leaves less unrelated material in the picture, and an explanation is written from the context around the activating positions, which carries more than the token alone. Figure 4(a) gives the token word cloud of expert 72 of layer 30, in which word is weighted by the gating mass the expert accumulates on it over the corpus. The words it puts forward are the, and, of and other function words. Such function tokens do carry varied and rich information [20], but that information resides in the features activated at their positions and cannot be 7 (a) routed tokens (b) routed tokens, MI reweighted (c) latent explanations Figure 4 Word clouds of expert 72 of layer 30, built from (a) routed tokens weighted by gating mass, (b) the same tokens reweighted by their contribution to mutual information without the top five function words, and (c) latent explanations. The algorithm theme of (c) is barely readable in (a) and (b). read off the tokens themselves, so at the token level they contribute nothing but noise. We remove the five most frequent function words1 and reweight each remaining token by its contribution to the mutual information between the expert and the token. Figure 4(b) is the result. It is more informative than Figure 4(a), yet part of what the expert does is still lost. Figure 4(c) is the explanation word cloud of the same expert, which shows that expert 72 is associated with two themes at once, exercise and health, and algorithms and data structures. The second theme is barely readable in Figure 4(b), because the latents that carry it activate only at particular positions within an algorithm. Latent F97783, for instance, activates only at the <= operator of binary search, and it is its explanation, Binary search loop condition, that ties it to binary search. On token word cloud this latent can contribute no more than the symbol <=, whose origin and meaning are left open.

sections.title: 5.2 Experts divide labor below the level of coarse domains
sections.content: Existing analyses of expert specialization ask whether experts align with domains such as code. Our explanation word clouds show that the model does not stop at this granularity. Inside single coarse domain we find experts that hold nearly disjoint parts of it, and the part each one holds is recognizable subfield rather than an arbitrary slice. Consider the code domain, for instance. Figure 3(a) and (b) show the explanation word clouds of experts 50 and 57, which both work on code. Expert 50 is Java expert. The words that take the largest font are Java, Android and imports, and the latents behind them are such things as Java import statements, JDBC generated keys and ButterKnife Android imports. Expert 57 is front-end web expert, carried by HTML, CSS and JavaScript together with the framework names React, Bootstrap and jQuery, and by latents about DOM events, CSS selectors and responsive layout.The same holds inside mathematics. Section gives experts 1 and 76. Expert 1 is geometry expert, dominated by geometry, coordinate, triangle and angle. Expert 76 instead concentrates on arithmetic and polynomial computation, with polynomial, matrix, division and decimal in the largest font, over latents such as Polynomial long division, and arbitrary-precision integers. To put number on the separation, we use GPT-5.5 to judge whether each latent explanation of an expert belongs to the corresponding theme, with the prompt reproduced in Section E. Table 2 reports the share of each experts explanations falling in the corresponding theme among the latents sampled from its dominant set. For example, 86.7% of the latent explanations in expert 50s dominant set relate to Java development. Against random sample of 2000 latents drawn from the dominant sets of the other 127 experts, the share of the same theme falls to between 1.9% and 6.7%.

The domains and their names are produced by GPT-5.5 from the expert labels alone. Section lists the experts of every domain. We do not fix the domains beforehand. Instead, we recover them by labeling each expert from its dominant-set word cloud and grouping those labels. The procedure has two steps, carried out by GPT-5.5. We first name each expert. We hand the model the words of one expert in the wordcloud together with their weights and ask for short label naming what that expert is responsible for, with the prompt in Section F. For instance, expert 50 receives Java and Android programming and expert 72 receives coding algorithms and musculoskeletal fitness, which recovers from the word cloud alone the two themes that Section 5.1 reads off it. We then group the experts. single call receives all 128 labels at once and returns partition of experts together with name for each part, with the prompt in Section G. We call these parts domains. Eleven domains come out of the 128 experts of layer 30, and Figure 5 gives the number of experts each of them holds. Section lists every expert with its label and its domain. The domains are internally diverse. Besides the Java and front-end experts of Section 5.2, computing holds experts on competitive programming (9, 40 and 118), system administration (51) and Python API documentation (113), each different part of working with code. The pairs of experts whose dominant sets overlap most (Section 4.3) fall inside domains. Of the 20 pairs with the largest at layer 30, 19 join two experts of the same domain, whereas only 12.8% of all expert pairs do. The two experts of such pair cover neighbouring ground, as with experts 83 and 105 on punctuation, 77 and 107 on mojibake, or 57 and 69 on JavaScript web programming. The one exception, experts 11 and 95, links LaTeX algebra in mathematics and reasoning with chemical and algebraic notation in applied science. Each label is written from the whole dominant set, so the shared latents enter both labels of pair. They make up median of only 12.3% of the dominant sets of these experts, however, so most of what each label is written from is not shared. The allocation across domains is strongly unequal. Computing takes 28 of the 128 experts and mathematics and reasoning takes 20, so these two domains alone hold 37.5% of the layer. Most of the labels in computing name code, the remainder covering such things as cybersecurity and software platforms, and mathematics and reasoning also takes in statistics, parts of the physical sciences and problem-solving reasoning. At the other 9 end the model spends very little on areas that human taxonomy would list in their own right. Art occurs in one label out of 128, that of expert 54, where it sits beside animals inside culture and recreation. Three of eleven domains (text form, language, and entities and identifiers) are not subject areas, and together they take 36 experts, or 28.1% of the layer. The largest of them, text form with 21 experts, is the second largest domain of the layer and covers document structure, punctuation, delimiters and encoding artifacts. All three are formed from the labels rather than requested. taxonomy of subject matter alone would have to spread these 36 experts over all of its categories, and would recover none of these domains as unit. One plausible source of the imbalance among the topical domains is the composition of the pretraining data, in which code and mathematics take share well above the one they occupy in general text. Llama 3, for instance, reports final data mix of roughly 25% mathematical and reasoning tokens and 17% code tokens against 50% of general knowledge [7].2 On this reading the allocation of experts across domains reflects the proportions of the corresponding domains in the training data. The model draws finer distinctions inside domain that occupies more of the data, and spends more of its experts on holding them.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We have proposed to study expert specialization in the feature space of an MoE layer instead of in taxonomy of domains fixed in advance. layer output is router-weighted sum of the outputs of the activated experts and the SAE encoder is affine in that output, so the pre-activation of every latent decomposes exactly over the experts that produced it. Tracing latents back through this decomposition yields, for each expert, the dominant set of latents whose activation it principally drives, which describes the expert in the models own vocabulary rather than in categories we supply. We apply this analysis to layers 4, 30 and 46 of Qwen3-30B-A3B, and our findings are the following. The contribution profile is markedly steeper than the gating profile that produces it, and the activation of latent is typically attributable to few experts rather than to all those that the router selects. Read from the expert side, most pairs of dominant sets share almost nothing, the overlap that exists concentrates on few pairs of experts, which at layer 30 almost always belong to the same domain, and about half of each experts set is its own. Interpreting the latents of these sets shows that the experts are specialized, and that the specialization sits below the granularity of conventional domain labels. Summarizing each experts dominant set into short label and grouping those labels into coarse domains shows that the allocation of experts across domains is uneven. The analysis needs only the expert outputs and an SAE on the layer output, so it applies to any MoE layer whose output is weighted sum of its experts, and can compare how routing objectives and load balancing losses shape the division of labor. The dominant sets also yield testable hypothesis for expert pruning, merging and feature-level steering, namely that removing or editing an expert chiefly affects the latents it dominates. We discuss the limitations of this work in Section A. 2The Qwen3 technical report does not disclose its data mixture, so we cannot check this on the model we study. Raising the proportion of code, mathematics and reasoning data is nonetheless common practice in current pretraining pipelines.

sections.title: A Limitations and future work
sections.content: Our analysis inherits the imperfections of the SAE. The reconstruction of the layer output carries an error, and the latents are not clean basis, since one feature can be split across several latents and can be absorbed into another [2]. better decomposition of an MLP into features would sharpen the picture of an MoE layer that we draw here. The pretraining mixture of Qwen3 is not disclosed, and our statistics are computed on corpus of our own choosing. What we measure is therefore routing on our data rather than on the data the model was trained on, and the reading of Section 5.3 that relates the allocation of experts to the proportions of domains in the training data remains conjecture. We report single model. Extending the analysis to more and to larger MoE models would show which of these observations are general, and the same instrument can be used to compare how different load balancing losses shape the division of labor among experts.

sections.title: B AI use statement
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools for implementing code, analyzing data, interpreting experimental results, and polishing the writing. Separately, GPT-5.5 is component of our method, used to explain latents, judge theme membership, label experts and group them into domains, with every prompt reproduced in Sections to and J. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.title: E Prompt to judge whether a latent belongs to a theme
sections.content: The theme name is substituted for {theme} in the prompt below, and the latent explanation is appended after the final line. The model is asked to answer only yes or no. The same prompt is used for the share row of Table 2 and for the random baseline, which draws 2000 latents from the dominant sets of every expert other than the one under study. 14 You are an expert in mechanistic interpretability, specializing in deciding whether Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) latent of large language model belongs to given theme. ## Background We study expert specialization in Qwen3-30B-A3B. Every MoE layer holds 128 experts. For each expert we recover the set of SAE latents whose activation that expert principally drives, and we interpret latents sampled from that set into short natural language explanation, noun phrase such as "Sailing knot names", "Origami folding steps" or "Falconry equipment terms". ## Task Decide whether the latent explanation below belongs to the theme named after this paragraph. Belonging means the explanation is about that theme, not merely adjacent to it or sharing generic word with it. For example, under the theme "Beekeeping", "Hive frame inspection" and "Queen bee marking" belong, while "Insect wing anatomy" and "Pollinator garden plants" do not, even though they are also about insects and flowers. The theme is: {theme} ## Output format Your response should contain only yes or no, in lowercase, with no other content. The feature explanation is:

sections.title: F Prompt to label an expert from its explanation word cloud
sections.content: The word cloud of an expert is passed to the model as one line per entry, of the form word: to the prompt below in decreasing order of weight. weight, appended You are an expert in mechanistic interpretability, specializing in describing what an individual expert of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model is responsible for. ## Background We study expert specialization in Qwen3-30B-A3B. Every MoE layer holds 128 experts, and router sends each token to few of them. To find out what an expert is responsible for we do not look at the tokens routed to it, because token is selected by the router but the information the expert adds lives in the features of the layer output. Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) with 2^20 latents is trained to reconstruct the output of one MoE layer, so each of its latents is one interpretable feature of what that layer computes. The activated part of latent is an affine function of the layer output, so the activation of latent decomposes exactly into sum of per-expert contributions. Averaging the normalized contribution over large corpus gives, for every expert and latent pair, the fraction of that latents activation the expert is responsible for. When this fraction is large we say the expert dominates the latent, and the set of all latents an expert dominates is its dominant set. Dominant sets are nearly disjoint across experts, so the dominant set of an expert is description of that expert alone. Latents sampled from each dominant set were separately interpreted by language model from activating contexts and logit effects. The result is short natural language explanation, noun phrase such as "Sailing knot names", "Origami folding steps" or "Falconry equipment terms". ## Input You are given the word cloud of one expert, built from the explanations of latents sampled from its dominant set. Each entry is word, or frequent two word collocation, together with weight. The weight is the frequency of that word among the explanations divided by the frequency of the most common word, so the heaviest entry always has weight 1.000. Common English stopwords have been removed, plural forms have been merged into their singulars, and at most 200 entries are listed in decreasing weight. This word cloud is the only evidence you have about the expert. You are seeing the vocabulary of the explanations rather than the explanations themselves, so it tells you which concepts recur and how often, but not how they combined inside any single latent. ## Task Name what this expert is responsible for, using at most nine words. - Weigh words by their weights and spend your attention on the heaviest ones. long tail of light words is normal and does not have to be covered. - Look for what sets this expert apart from an arbitrary other expert. Words such as code, text, term, terminology, description, name, reference and value are frequent in many experts and are weak evidence on their own. Prefer the words that would be surprising in random expert. 15 - Say what the expert is about instead of concatenating its heaviest words. For an expert whose cloud is led by hive, honey, beeswax and queen, "hive, honey, beeswax, queen" is bad answer and "beekeeping" is good one. - You are not choosing from fixed list of topics. An expert may specialize along an axis that is not subject area at all. Name that axis when that is what the cloud shows. - few experts carry several unrelated themes at once. When the heavy words clearly split into separate groups, name each group and join them with "and", for instance "beekeeping and origami". The nine word limit binds here, so keep every theme to one or two words, and when the groups do not all fit, keep the heaviest ones and drop the rest. Do not force one label onto such an expert, and do not invent second theme when the cloud only supports one. - Be as specific as the evidence allows and no more specific than that. If the cloud is about geometry, say geometry rather than mathematics. If it spreads over several unrelated parts of mathematics, say mathematics. ## Output format Your response should contain only the label with no other content. Write noun phrase of at most nine words, with no trailing punctuation and no quotation marks. Keep the capitalization of proper nouns such as Kyoto, UNESCO and Darwin, and leave every other word in lowercase. The word cloud of this expert is:

sections.title: G Prompt to group the experts into domains
sections.content: The 128 labels are appended to the prompt below as one line per expert, of the form E{expert id}: {label}. The only quantities we set are the bounds on the number of groups, between 6 and 13, and the returned number of groups, eleven, falls strictly inside them. The prompt fixes the level of grouping but names no domain that the partition should contain. You are an expert in mechanistic interpretability, working on the division of labor among the experts of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model. ## Background We study expert specialization in Qwen3-30B-A3B. One MoE layer holds 128 experts, and router sends each token to few of them. For every expert we recovered the set of Sparse Autoencoder latents whose activation that expert is chiefly responsible for, we interpreted latents sampled from that set into short natural language explanations, and we summarized those explanations into one short label naming what the expert is responsible for. Those 128 labels are the input below, one per expert. The labels were written independently of one another, so their wording is not standardized. Two experts can hold closely related responsibilities while sharing no word, and two labels can share generic word such as terminology, description or reference while describing responsibilities that have nothing to do with each other. Read for what an expert does rather than for surface overlap. This grouping asks coarse question. Group at the coarsest level the labels still support, and leave the internal structure of group alone. ## Task Partition the 128 experts into between 6 and 13 groups, aiming for about 10. - Every expert belongs to exactly one group and all 128 experts are placed. Nothing may be dropped and nothing may appear twice. - group is good when its name is true of every expert in it. Among the names that stay true, take the most general one rather than the most specific, and prefer one large group under general name over several small groups under specific ones. - There is no upper bound on the size of group, and group sizes do not need to be balanced. Do not split group into subfields merely to even out the sizes. - Do not cut small coherent domain apart either, and do not manufacture groups merely to reach the group count. - group may be organized around any responsibility its members share. - Many labels name two or three themes at once. Place such an expert by the theme that carries most of its label, preferring theme that already has home among the other experts. Do not open group for single odd pairing. - Keep one axis in one place. Two experts responsible for the same kind of thing belong in the same group even when their labels attach that thing to different subject matter, so do not leave near duplicates of single theme sitting in two different groups. - Avoid catch-all group. group is catch-all whenever some of its members lack the property its name states, and giving that group specific sounding name does not repair it. Check every group by walking its members one at time and asking whether the name is true of that member, then move out the ones for which it is not. If few experts genuinely fit nowhere they may share one residual group, which must stay small and must be named for something its members actually have in common. - Name each group as generally and as briefly as you can, one or two words wherever the group allows it. Two closely related things may be joined with and. What is not acceptable is name that enumerates three or more subject areas, of the shape "A, B, and C", because such name states no organizing principle at all. When the only name you can find for candidate group is list of that shape, either find the more general word that covers the list, 16 or split the group along the very boundaries the list names. ## Output format Respond with JSON and nothing else. No prose before or after it and no markdown code fence. The JSON is list of objects ordered from the largest group to the smallest, each object having exactly two fields: - "group", the name of the group - "experts", the ids of the experts in that group, as integers in ascending order The shape of the response is [{"group": "<name of the largest group>", "experts": [0, 7, 19]}, {"group": "<name of the next group>", "experts": [3, 12]}] The 128 expert labels are:

sections.title: I SAE training details
sections.content: We trained our SAE with the latent size of 220 = 1, 048, 576 on the layer 4,30,46 MoE layer output stream of Qwen3-30B-A3B [19] independently. Activations were collected from mixture of pre-training and post-training data taken from the Olmo 3 [15] training corpus: 5/8 from pre-training data, 1/4 from reasoning chain-of-thought dataset, 1/8 from an instruction-following supervised fine-tuning dataset. In order to increase the diversity of the activation sources within single batch, we dumped all the activations before training. For each example in the dataset, we ran forward pass of the LLM to obtain the MoE activations and then sampled only 512 of them from that example into the pool, discarding the remaining activations. For each training-batch, we drew batch from activations we dumped uniformly at random without replacement. Our hyperparameters are set following the common practice. We used square-root warmup followed by linear decay. During the first 100 steps, the learning rate is warmed up from 0.1ηmax to the peak value ηmax following square-root schedule, i.e., η(t) = η0 + (ηmax η0)(cid:112)t/100 with η0 = 0.1ηmax. The learning rate then linearly decays from ηmax to η0 during the remainder of training. We set ηmax = 8 105. We trained the SAE with the AdamW optimizer [12] with (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.999) and weight decay of 0.01. We used 19 Table 4 The FVU of our SAE on each layer. Layer FVU 4 12.6% 30 25.1% 46 7.6% batch size of 8192 and trained each SAE on about 3.2B tokens. Our initialization setup generally follows Conerly et al. [3] and Ameisen et al. [1]. Let = 2048 be the hidden size of LLM, and = 1, 048, 576 be the latent size of SAE. We normalize the activations to n, where denotes the activations of the given layer. n, i.e., [X] = After normalization, we filter out activations whose norm exceeds 20 times the batch-wise mean, as such outliers would destabilize training. We initialized every entry of the encoder matrix from U( 1 , 1 ) and every entry of Wdec from U( 1 , 1 ). Our SAE is trained with activation function TopK. For the number of activations κ retained by the activation function, we set κ = 1000 initially, and let κ linearly decay to 100 during the first 10,000 steps, after which it is held constant. We used an auxiliary loss following Gao et al. [6] and Deng et al. [4] with the coefficient of 1/32. The auxiliary loss always uses the same value of κ as our main activation function. After training we normalize each column of Wdec to unit norm and rescale the corresponding row of Wenc by the reciprocal factor, which yields an equivalent SAE. We likewise fold the activation normalization factor into the weights, so the exported SAE applies directly to the raw layer output as in Equations (2) and (3). We use fraction of variance unexplained (FVU) to evaluate our SAE. The FVU values of each layer are shown in Table 4. Consistent with Gao et al. [6], we also observe that the intermediate layers of LLMs are more difficult to reconstruct using SAE, compared with both shallow and deep layers. Pipeline of auto-interpretability Following common practice, we use an LLM to produce natural-language explanation for each latent. Unlike prior work that relies primarily on activated contexts, we provide the explainer with three sources of evidence: (i) activated contexts, (ii) logit effects, and (iii) layer information. Activated contexts. We run inference on the 1.5B-token validation set of Section 4, which does not overlap with the SAE training data. For each latent, we collect all activated contexts within 64-token window and select the top 5 by activation strength. We additionally sample 5 contexts uniformly at random from the remaining activations. We found that top-activating contexts are often highly similar to one another, which biases the explainer toward the literal surface pattern shared by those examples. Adding randomly sampled contexts increases diversity and encourages the explainer to summarize the latents more general function rather than its most salient literal trigger. All ten contexts, along with their token-level activation values, are provided to the explainer. Logit effects. To quantify latents direct effect on the output distribution, we apply the logit lens, projecting the latents decoder vector through the LM head and extracting the top-10 boosted and top-10 suppressed tokens by logit value. Boosted tokens indicate what the latent promotes, while suppressed tokens indicate what it suppresses. Layer information. We also tell the explainer the total number of layers, the layer at which the latent lives, and its relative depth, together with soft prior on how features are typically distributed across depth: shallow layers tend to contain input features that respond to specific tokens, local syntax, or surface patterns; middle layers tend to contain abstract features that capture discourse patterns, reasoning states, or semantic categories; and deep layers tend to contain output features that directly shape next-token prediction. This prior guides how the explainer weighs the evidence but is explicitly framed as tiebreaker rather than constraint. For input features, activated contexts are usually sufficient; for output features, the logit effects are more informative, since their activated contexts are often diffuse; for abstract features in the middle layers, neither source alone is typically conclusive, and the explainer is instructed to combine both. For output features, we adopt fixed naming convention (Say for boosted tokens and Dont Say for suppressed tokens) so that output-oriented explanations are easily distinguishable from concept-level ones. 20 Output format. In addition to concise explanation phrase, we ask the explainer to report confidence rating on three-level scale (High, Medium, Low) reflecting how well the provided evidence supports its explanation. The explainer is also allowed to output Uninterpretable when the activated contexts and logit effects do not exhibit consistent, describable pattern, rather than being forced to produce speculative explanation. The full system prompt and user prompt are given in Section J.1. J.1 Prompts We provide the full system prompt and user prompt template below. In the user prompt, fields in double braces are filled in per latent. You are an expert in mechanistic interpretability, specializing in interpreting features extracted by Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) from large language model. ## Task Given one SAE feature, infer the concept, behavior, pattern, or output tendency it represents. Produce: 1. concise interpretation phrase (2-6 words preferred; clarity > brevity). 2. confidence rating. --- ## Input You may receive up to three sections. Any may be missing. ### 1. Context Activations Text examples that strongly activate the feature, with token-level activation highlights. [Context 1] [Text] "The cat sat on the mat in Paris" [/Text] Top Activations: [mat0.92] [Paris0.87] [/Context 1] How to read them: - Global pass: identify topic, domain, task, language, register, formatting, or discourse situation shared across examples. - Local pass: examine the highest-activating tokens -- do they share semantic field, syntactic role, position, or discourse function? - Cross-example pass: isolate the single common thread that explains every activation. Reject hypotheses contradicted by any example. ### 2. Logit Effect The features output influence at its own layer, presented as direct logit-lens projection of the decoder vector: list of boosted / suppressed tokens. Use it to infer what the feature pushes the model to say or avoid saying. Logit effects can be noisy (especially in earlier layers), so weight context activations more heavily when they are clearer. ### 3. Layer Information Soft prior based on layer depth: - Shallow -> surface features: lexical items, local syntax, formatting, named entities, languages, domain terminology. - Middle -> abstract / behavioral features: discourse patterns, reasoning states, task structure, style, intent, semantic categories. - Deep -> output-oriented features: answer formats, completion templates, specific phrases, refusal / compliance, "say X" behaviors. The layer prior is tiebreaker, not constraint. Override it whenever activations or logit effects give stronger evidence. --- ## Reasoning Procedure 1. Activations -- what topic / pattern, which tokens, what common thread? 2. Logit effect -- what is boosted, what is suppressed, is there clear output push? 3. Layer prior -- what type of feature does the depth suggest? 4. Synthesis: - Activations + logit effect agree -> combine into one label. - They diverge -> take the clearer signal; do not force unified story. - Both incoherent -> output Uninterpretable. 5. Phrase -- specific, 2-6 words, no filler. 21 6. Confidence -- see scale below. --- ## Output Format Output only the two tags below. No reasoning, preamble, or commentary. <explanation>concise interpretation phrase</explanation> <confidence>High Medium Low</confidence> Confidence scale: - High -- activations and logit effect are coherent, repeated, and specific. - Medium -- plausible interpretation; some evidence is partial, noisy, or only one channel is clear. - Low -- weak, sparse, or contradictory evidence; label is tentative. If evidence is too noisy, contradictory, or insufficient, output exactly: <explanation>Uninterpretable</explanation> <confidence>Low</confidence> --- ## Label Conventions ### Surface features (shallow) Name the concept or pattern directly. - European capitals - medical terminology - Python indentation - Chinese punctuation - HTML attribute syntax ### Behavioral features (middle) Name the behavior, capability, discourse function, or abstract state. - formal register - negation logic - Chinese language response - step-by-step reasoning - instruction-following mode - uncertainty expression ### Output-oriented features (deep) - Boosted output -> prefix with Say: Say however, Say comma, Say closing parenthesis, Say final answer. - Suppressed output -> prefix with Dont Say: Dont Say period, Dont Say apology, Dont Say the. Do not substitute Produce, Express, Output, Generate, etc. for Say. --- ## Specificity Rules Be precise. Replace vague labels with concrete ones: Prefer Avoid ------------------------------------------------------- locations science-related punctuation tokens sentence-ending punctuation negative words medical stuff negation / denial medical symptom description European capitals scientific terminology Banned patterns: xxx-related, xxx tokens, xxx words, xxx stuff, xxx things, and meta-descriptions of the feature itself (e.g. activates on nouns, high activation feature). --- ## Honesty Rule Do not fabricate coherence. When evidence does not support specific interpretation, output the Uninterpretable template above. Forced labels are worse than honest abstention. ## Context Activations Two complementary sets of examples are provided: the strongest (top) activations and random sample. Read both -- the random set guards against over-fitting to the most extreme cases. 22 ### Top Activating Contexts The 5 examples where this feature fires most strongly. [Top Context 1] [Text] {{top_context_1.text}} [/Text] Top Activations: {{top_context_1.top_activations}} [/Top Context 1] ... (Top Context 2-5 in the same format) ### Random Contexts 5 examples sampled at random from this features activating set (a less-biased view of where it fires). [Random Context 1] [Text] {{random_context_1.text}} [/Text] Top Activations: {{random_context_1.top_activations}} [/Random Context 1] ... (Random Context 2-5 in the same format) ## Logit Effect Source: decoder-vector projection. This feature lives at layer {{layer_idx}} (single decoder; SAE-style). Decoder L2 norm = {{decoder_l2_norm}} Top 10 boosted logits: Rank 1: [{{token}}], logit={{logit}} ... (Rank 2-10) Top 10 suppressed logits: Rank 1: [{{token}}], logit={{logit}} ... (Rank 2-10) ## Model Information Model: {{model_name}} -- {{num_layers}} transformer layers (0-indexed). Feature extractor: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE), trained at layer {{layer_idx}}. Each feature has single decoder vector at its own layer. ## Layer Information The model has {{num_layers}} layers in total (0-indexed); the current features layer index is {{layer_idx}} (relative depth {{layer_idx / num_layers}}). Use the relative position as soft prior, but override it with the logit-effect signal whenever the two disagree. Analyze the context activations, logit effect, and model / layer information, then respond in the exact output format specified in the system prompt above.
